#677. Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO

Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.

The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility, each more than 500 meters (1,640 feet) long, look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles), allowing Russia to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," Malinionis added.

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals, citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.

"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.

"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.

"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE defense company sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.

"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.

The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.

"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."

Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.

The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

#676. A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms

A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.

The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.

The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?

Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance

To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.

At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.

The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.

Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.

Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.

A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans

One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.

The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).

This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.

"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."

Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.

Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.

One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.

"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."

There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.

In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.

Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?

The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.

Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.

Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.

For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.

"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

Authorship: In addition to Sperling and Buckley, Mass General Brigham authors include Diana L. Townsend, Colin J. Birkenbihl, Madison Cuppels, Gillian T. Coughlan, Mabel T. Seto, Jane A. #675. HBO’s Harry Potter Cast vs. the Movies: See Every Character Side by Side

Here are the new Harry Potter cast members side by side with the actors who played the characters in the Warner Bros. movies.

It’s been only 15 years since Warner Bros. released Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, yet a fresh adaptation of J.K. Rowling’s massively popular novels is coming this Christmas.

For HBO’s new TV series version of the Harry Potter saga, each book following the boy wizard’s Hogwarts journey being adapted into a full season. The major roles from Rowling’s first two novels — Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone and Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets — has been recast with different actors than those who played the characters in the Warner Bros. films. The adult actors are often much younger than their film counterparts, as the show is sticking closer to the characters’ ages in the books.

Below are all the actors who have been announced, with photos showing them side by side with their film version counterparts.

Movies: Daniel Radcliffe / Show: Dominic McLaughlin

Movies: Emma Watson / Show: Arabella Stanton

Movies: Rubert Grint / Show: Alastair Stout

(Or, if we’re being formal about things: Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore).

The movies: Richard Harris and Michael-Gambon / Show: John Lithgow

Movies: Maggie Smith / Show: Janet McTeer

Movies: Alan Rickman / Show: Paapa Essiedu

Movies: Robbie Coltrane / Show: Nick Frost

Movies: Julie Walters / Show: Katherine Parkinson

Movies: Jason Isaacs / Show: Johnny Flynn

Lucius doesn’t appear in the first Harry Potter film (or book), but he’s one of a few characters that are among the first season’s cast that don’t show up until later in the film series (others include Parvati Patil and Cornelius Fudge).

Movies: Matthew Lewis / Show: Rory Wilmot

Movies: Harry Melling / Show: Amos Kitson

Movies: James and Oliver Phelps / Show: Tristan and Gabriel Harland

Movies: Bonnie Wright / Show: Gracie Cochrane for season one and Bonnie Hill for season two — the first recasting of the series.

Movies: Chris Rankin / Show: Ruari Spooner

Movies: Zoe Wanamaker / Show: Louise Brealey

Movies: Shefali Chowdhury and Alessia Leoni

Movies: Richard Griffiths, Fiona Shaw / Show: Daniel Rigby, Bel Powley

Movies: Robert Hardy / Show: Bertie Carvel

Movies: David Bradley / Show: Paul Whitehouse

Movies: Geraldine Somerville / Show: Hannah Chinn

Movies: Adrian Rawlins / Show: Jasper Talbot (both Lily and James are closer to the ages in the books — 21 — than the actors in the films)

Movie: Warwick Davis / Show: Also Warwick Davis! The only original cast member to return and reprise their movie role.

Movies: Christian Coulson, Show: Billy Barratt (for season two of the Harry Potter series based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets)

Movies: Shirley Henderson / Show: Molly Hewitt (for season two)

Movies: Hugh Mitchell / Show: Jasper Ambrose

Movies: Kenneth Branagh / Show: Kit Harington (season two)

Nobody has yet been announced for the franchise’s biggest villain, but an interesting question is: When will the main actor for the role first show up? In the films, Fiennes didn’t appear until the forth movie, Goblet of Fire, as that’s when Voldemort first takes human form. But his face appears at the end of the first film (played by Richard Bremmer), and in the second film, he appears as his younger self, Tom Riddle (played by Christian Peter Coulson). Given the production has cast several roles that didn’t appear until the latter films, it wouldn’t be at all surprising if the production has quietly already cast an actor to play Voldemort throughout the entire series.

#673. Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review — how good is this budget lens for astrophotography?

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) is an impressive lens for the price and certainly won’t break the bank. Image quality is impressive but imperfect, yet it's still an attractive lens.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Budget primes can be, surprisingly, excellent choices for photographers shooting all subjects. It’s all too easy to get carried away with the best specs, such as a large maximum aperture and impressive optical design often seen in more expensive options. But affordable lenses like the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) have the potential to impress and delight in equal measure.

The 35mm f/1.8 is a compact and lightweight lens offering a reasonably fast maximum aperture, making it a prime candidate for astrophotography. It’s also the same size and almost the same weight as the Viltrox AF 55mm f/1.8 FE (APO), another lens that could potentially grace your camera bag.

With a highly attractive price tag of just $399 / £385, and mount options for Nikon Z and Sony FE, many astrophotographers will be wondering if this is a lens worth considering. It features 13 elements in 10 groups, as well as featuring an apochromatic (APO) design for reducing chromatic aberration as much as possible. As much as possible is key here because not all lenses are as successful as the manufacturer claims, although that’s not a comment on the 35mm f/1.8. Read on to discover if this could be one of the best lenses for astrophotography.

For a budget lens, the 35mm f/1.8 produces great, yet not perfect, image quality. On the plus side, images are nice and sharp, particularly in the centre, even when shooting wide open at f/1.8. At this aperture setting, though, there is some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. This is a surprise since it’s an APO lens, and, equally surprising, it’s isolated, but it is something you have to consider.

You do have to zoom into the image to see it, so it may not be a dealbreaker. Photos shot at f/1.8 are sharpest in the centre, with some fall-off towards the edges, with the corners exhibiting the least sharpness. There’s also the strongest vignetting at f/1.8. At the time of writing, there’s no Adobe Lightroom lens profile for the lens, but you can manually remove the vignetting and even create a preset of your own.

The vignette disappears as soon as f/4, with a gradual increase in sharpness across the frame between f/2.8 and f/5.6. f/8 and f/11 appear identical in terms of sharpness and occupy the sweet spot, while diffraction is clearly at work when you stop down to f/16. In reality, it’s unlikely you’d shoot beyond f/11 with this lens, even if you were shooting landscapes.

Overall, image quality is impressive despite not being perfect and stopping down to f/2.8 when shooting astro does provide greater clarity across the frame. This is, as you know, at the expense of having to shoot at a slightly higher ISO setting to compensate.

While f/1.8 lenses may not have the speed and light-gathering capabilities of faster f/1.4 and f/1.2 lenses, they’re considerably smaller and lighter. The lens only has a 58mm filter thread, so if you use any night filters, they will be at the less expensive end of the price scale.

For some photographers, the slight speed reduction of f/1.8 is a worthy compromise, and at 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm with a weight of 12.52 oz / 355 g, the 35mm f/1.8 is beautifully compact and balances well with camera bodies.

Build quality is excellent, and it’s fair to say the lens belies its budget price tag. The metal build alongside the manual aperture ring gives the 35mm f/1.8 a much more premium look and feel.

The aperture ring can also be set to A for in-body aperture adjustments, as well as offering the ability to switch the aperture click on and off. The latter is most popular with videographers. There’s also a customizable Fn button on the side.

The lens is weather-sealed against light rain and dust, with a rubber gasket on the lens mount. The front element also features a water and smudge-resistant coating, which is certainly useful for outdoor photography. Plus, there’s a minimum focusing distance of just 13.4 in / 34 cm, which is useful for daylight photography but of no consequence for astrophotography.

The 35mm f/1.8 is made up of 13 elements in 10 groups, and as previously mentioned, features an APO design, which is intended to eliminate chromatic aberration in high-contrast scenes.

The elements include two extra-low dispersion (ED), three high refractive index (HR) and one ultra aspherical (UA). The UA lens is claimed to be Viltrox’s LAB Series quality, which matches the Viltrox flagship line-up.

When it comes to features, prime lenses are always pretty basic, with few features to shout about. The 35mm f/1.8 is certainly no exception, but its build quality and overall design hold up alongside its image quality and reasonably fast maximum aperture. It does, however, have a few points worth mentioning.

One feature that many Viltrox lenses have, including the 35mm f/1.8, is a USB-C Port on the lens mount. This allows you to use a smartphone app or a desktop app to quickly and easily update firmware. This is so much easier than having to download a file to your memory card and installing lens updates via the camera, which is how most native lenses have to be updated.

The manual aperture ring features click and clickless operation via a switch on the side, so you can easily see what aperture you’re using at a glance. The focusing ring is smooth and offers comfortable resistance, making manual focus a breeze. It’s also wide enough to rotate using gloves, although, being a compact lens, it’s narrower than what you’d expect on a larger and faster prime lens.

Autofocus (AF) is reasonably fast and silent, being powered by an stepping motor (STM). The AF performance seemed to improve after the firmware update that was installed via the desktop app before testing fully commenced.

This functionality isn’t, of course, relevant to astrophotography, but it’s still a useful point to mention in case you intend to use the lens with autofocus in the day. Focusing is also internal, so the front element doesn’t rotate during focusing like cheap and cheerful kit lenses.

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) was tested with the Sony A7R V, which offers an unforgivingly high resolution. The lens was tested at night with a focus on astrophotography, and in daylight to assess sharpness, distortion and general functionality for an all-round approach to testing.

Online reviews echo one another, praising the AF 35mm f/1.8 for its sharpness and cost. Users appreciate that while it’s certainly not in the league of Sony’s premium G Master lenses, it represents great value for money. Some reviewers mention great build quality and looking good when paired with their Sony camera.

✅ You’re on a tight budget: The price of this lens is extremely attractive given the specs and performance.

✅ You want portability: This is a compact and lightweight lens that's much less bulky than faster primes.

❌ You want the best: This is a great little lens in many ways, but its image quality isn't the best that money can buy.

❌ You shoot APS-C: Unless this is what you want, the equivalent focal length on a crop sensor is 52.5mm

Prime lenses can be expensive, especially if you’re looking at those with an f/1.4 or f/1.2 maximum aperture. The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 FE (APO) is a budget option in the Viltrox line-up, but with decent overall performance alongside impressive image quality for the price, this is a great 35mm lens for those on a budget. It’s also compact and lightweight, which could be useful if you often head out shooting with several lenses in your kit bag.

Just going back to image quality, images are sharp, but when shooting astrophotography at f/1.8, there was some astigmatism at the left edges of the frame. This is where stars appear as crosses. You can only really see this when you zoom in to 100%, but it’s worth bearing in mind if you’re looking for the closest to optical perfection you can find.

When a weather-sealed prime lens with a manual aperture ring costs just $399 / £385, you can’t help but take notice. Build quality is excellent and the lens undoubtedly looks and feels like it would be more expensive than it is.

Considering all of this and the image quality, the lens is fairly priced and is still at the release price, so it could become more affordable in the future. Just like other Viltrox lenses, in the box you get the lens, a lens hood, front and rear lens caps and a soft lens case.

The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.2 LAB FE is part of Viltrox’s flagship lens series and offers a much faster maximum aperture, as the name suggests. It’s also more expensive, larger and heavier.

If you’d like a wider lens, the Sony FE 20mm f/1.8 G is a fantastic option offering exceptional image quality alongside a compact build and light weight. A potential must-have for Sony users.

If you’d like to go wider still, the Sigma 14mm f/1.4 DG DN Art is an absolute beast of a lens, offering an ultra-wide light-gathering field of view alongside a fast f/1.4 maximum aperture.

#672. Live Nation Reports $10.1 Billion In Revenue In Jump From Last Year

"Artists are taking their music to more fans in more places than ever, and fans are showing up in record numbers," CEO Michael Rapino said in a statement.

Live Nation posted a record-high $10.1 billion in revenue for the company’s third quarter, the live music giant reported on Thursday, buoyed by the company’s growing international business.

The $10.1 billion figure marks a 19 percent increase from 2025, while the company reported $892 million in operating income, a 13 percent jump from last year. Fan attendance overall grew 19 percent to 61 million people, Live Nation said, with international attendance growing 29 percent and accounting for 60 percent of the company’s total fan growth.

The company’s concerts division reported $8.7 billion in revenue for the quarter, with about $602.9 million in income, while ticketing reported $870 million in revenue and over $315 million in operating income. Live Nation’s sponsorship and advertising division posted nearly $506 million in revenue and over $350 million in income.

Live Nation also posted $3.8 billion in deferred revenue, an eight percent increase from last year.

“In a world of endless screens and AI-generated everything, the one thing that can’t be replicated is being there,” Live Nation CEO Michael Rapino said in a statement, adding that the company expects 180 million fans in attendance through 2026. “Artists are taking their music to more fans in more places than ever, and fans are showing up in record numbers.“

#671. The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?

Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions.

Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics.

Published in Science Advances, the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years.

The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges.

Why Crocodiles Survived the Dinosaur Extinction

The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover.

Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact.

Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group.

"Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out."

The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions.

Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles.

The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton.

Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus, a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus, was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four.

Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug.

"Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate."

Fossils Reveal 245 Million Years of Climate History

To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today.

The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history.

A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled.

About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica.

Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions.

Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions.

During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times.

A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments.

These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions.

What Happened After the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid?

The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs.

They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions.

When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption.

However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely.

Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles.

Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs.

The Survival Strategy That Could Now Become a Weakness

The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction.

Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat.

The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change.

For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move.

Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder."

The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC).

"Star Trek" celebrated its diamond anniversary last month, marking 60 years since it first aired on NBC on Sept. 8, 1966. There were a bunch of Trekkie-themed celebrations and news stories over September, including festive documentaries, special screenings, tributes, parade floats, interviews, and even a Galileo shuttle story.

Now, publishers Penguin Random House and Ten Speed Press are releasing "Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History" on Nov. 10, 2026.

This coffee table book promises unprecedented exploration of the pioneering space fantasy television series and enduring pop culture property that bolstered the space race and ignited sci-fi audiences' imaginations by taking us to strange new worlds and civilizations in the final frontier.

It's a striking 416-page hardback written by Kyle Newman and Jeff Bond, documenting all the classic characters and plotlines that are still inspiring artists, filmmakers, authors, and astronauts around the globe six decades later, and we’ve got our hands on a primo copy to show off.

"When the original 'Star Trek' series burst onto the screen in 1966, few could have anticipated the enduring legacy it would create," states the synopsis.

"Although it lasted just three seasons and 79 episodes, 'Star Trek' left an indelible mark on popular culture, and it soon spawned an animated television series, a blockbuster major motion picture franchise, and for its most dedicated fans, a way of life.

"The story of the U.S.S. Enterprise and her crew—James T. Kirk (William Shatner), Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Leonard McCoy (DeForest Kelley), Montgomery Scott (James Doohan), Nyota Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), Pavel Chekov (Walter Koenig), and Hikaru Sulu (George Takei)—as well as the behind-the-scenes story of its creators, The Great Bird of the Galaxy Gene Roddenberry and his many collaborators, is extraordinary."

Inside this classy collector's edition, which is the first volume of a two-book series gazing back at the complete history of "Star Trek," readers will behold a wealth of archival photos, costumes, storyboards, cast and creators' chats, behind-the-scenes ephemera, props, and filming models.

"Star Trek: The Original Voyages" chronicles not just the iconic TV show but also the short-lived animated series and all six of the big-screen "Star Trek" feature films up to the year 1991.

Above and beyond the dramatic cover emblazoned with reflective lettering, this beefy "Trek" book truly leaps into warp speed, covering all the licensed toys, comic books, convention memorabilia, media parodies, promotional roadshows, trading cards, and vintage magazine covers.

"Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History" lands on Nov. 10, 2026.

Boldly celebrate 60 years of Star Trek with this official visual history of the original series, documenting how its iconic characters and storylines reshaped the science fiction genre.

From stellar pulsations to giant dust clouds and a mysterious companion, astronomers are piecing together why Betelguese keeps changing brightness.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Betelguese, one of the brightest stars in the night sky, has been putting on quite a show lately — but not in the way you might expect.

The famous red supergiant in the constellation Orion has been growing noticeably fainter in recent months.

Of the 21 brightest stars in the night sky, Betelgeuse is perhaps the most enigmatic. Its changing brightness poses a puzzle: how do the star's pulsations, dust eruptions, and a possible companion contribute to its fading?

Even the translation of Betelgeuse's name is contentious. For a long time, it was thought to be a corruption of three Arabic words, usually translated as "The Armpit of the Giant." However, other experts in star nomenclature now dispute that interpretation, proposing instead "The Hand of al-Jauzā," with al-Jauzā referring to Orion.

Although classified as a red supergiant, Betelgeuse usually appears more orange than red— golden orange or deep topaz. It is one of the most famous stars in its class. Henry M. Neely (1877-1963), for many years a popular lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium, described its restless behavior in his book A Primer for Stargazers:

"(Betelgeuse) expands and contracts spasmodically, like an old man with his strength almost entirely spent, panting in the asthmatic decrepitude of old age."

Betelgeuse naturally expands and contracts like a beating heart. As an aging red supergiant, it has a regular pulsation cycle of roughly 430 days: when it expands, its outer layers cool and it dims; when it contracts, they heat up and it brightens. Among first-magnitude stars — the brightest category of stars in the night sky — it is the only marked variable. Its scale is equally remarkable: located 650 light-years away, Betelgeuse is among the largest and most luminous stars of its class, with a luminosity of about 14,000 suns at maximum and 7,600 suns at minimum. Only a few such objects have been identified in our galaxy.

British astronomer Sir John Herschel (1792-1871) first noticed Betelgeuse's variability beginning in 1836. Astronomers describe apparent brightness using magnitude: lower numbers mean brighter stars. In April 2023, Betelgeuse reached magnitude 0.0 — as bright as Vega, the fifth brightest star. At minimum brightness, such as in 1927 and 1941, its magnitude may fall to +1.2, making it appear about three times fainter.

Three threads run through this mystery: Betelgeuse's roughly 430-day pulsation, its much longer recurring dimming cycle, and the exceptional Great Dimming of 2019—2020. Keeping them, separate helps explain why one cause need not account for every change in brightness.

Alongside its roughly 430-day pulsation, Betelgeuse shows a mysterious 2,100-day (5.75-year) dimming cycle. Known as a "Long Secondary Period," this longer cycle puzzled astronomers for a century. Some suggested that one or more stars might orbit Betelgeuse; others found no evidence for such companions or actively refuted their existence.

At long last, in January 2026, researchers using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT) located in on Cerro Paranal in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile and NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, published the clearest images and direct evidence of a faint companion star orbiting the red supergiant. Formally named Alpha Ori B, Jared Goldberg, an astrophysicist researching the phenomenon, nicknamed the companion star "Betelbuddy," though in deference to the new definition of Betelgeuse's name meaning "the hand of al-Jawzā," the name Siwarha was ultimately chosen for the probable companion star, which means her bracelet in Arabic.

In this explanation, Siwarha orbits deep within Betelgeuse's outer chromosphere, a layer of its atmosphere, circling about every six years. As it moves through gas and dust ejected by the supergiant, its gravity creates a dense wake of gas, with ripples and shockwaves that disrupt stellar winds and mass loss. When the concentrated dust trail passes between Earth and Betelgeuse, it can make the main star appear decidedly dimmer.

Betelgeuse recently experienced another sharp drop in brightness. Since this past August, it has faded from magnitude +0.5 to +0.95 and now appears just a trifle dimmer than the similarly hued orange star Aldebaran in Taurus the Bull. This decline may be another example of the dimming described above, although the brightness change alone does not establish its cause.

Aldebaran can be used as a comparison to Betelgeuse, since they both happen to be in the general vicinity of each other. If you want to make such a determination yourself, keep in mind that Aldebaran currently rises in the east-northeast before 7 p.m. local standard time, followed about 90 minutes later by Betelgeuse, which will emerge from beyond the eastern horizon. By 11:30 p.m., both stars will be well placed for viewing in the east-southeast part of the sky.

Betelgeuse marks Orion's right shoulder. To locate Aldebaran, look for the three bright, evenly spaced stars that form Orion's belt. Draw an imaginary line through the three belt stars and extend it upwards and to the right. Follow that line for about two fists' width at arm's length (roughly 22 degrees) until you hit a sideways, V-shaped cluster of stars known as the Hyades, which forms the face of Taurus. Aldebaran sits right at one end of that V-shape, glowing with a distinct orange-red color as the "angry eye" of the bull charging toward Orion.

View them late tonight; which star appears brighter?

The changes visible now invite comparison with a far more dramatic episode: The Great Dimming Event of 2019—2020.

Between October 2019 and February 2020, Betelgeuse experienced an unprecedented, dramatic plunge in brightness — losing over two-thirds of its luster, falling from magnitude +0.5 to +1.7; the rank of a second magnitude star. It then returned to a more normal brightness, reaching an unusually bright peak of 0.0 by the spring of 2023. While the sudden dimming caused internet and media speculation that Betelgeuse was about to die as a spectacular supernova, infrared structural and chemical models showed no significant change in the star's luminosity; Betelgeuse was still firmly in its helium-burning phase and is expected to live for another 100,000 to perhaps many hundreds of thousands of years before it explodes.

So, what caused The Great Dimming? The mystery was ultimately solved by compiling data from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground observatories.

Apparently, Betelgeuse "sneezed." A massive bubble of superhot plasma rose from a giant convection cell inside the star and blasted into space. As this ejected gas moved millions of miles away from the star, it cooled rapidly and condensed into solid silicon monoxide dust. This giant stardust cloud acted like a literal screen, blocking a substantial portion of the star's light from our viewpoint. This event was exacerbated because the massive eruption perfectly aligned with the lowest point of the star's 430-day pulsation cycle as well as the orbital interference of the companion star Siwarha.

From the standpoint of producing the absolute maximum possible dimming of Betelgeuse, this cosmic trifecta was the perfect storm!

Betelgeuse has long been known as a variable star, and recent breakthroughs are helping astronomers untangle its erratic behavior. Internal pulsations and massive dust eruptions contribute to its changing brightness, while gravitational interactions with the newly reported, probable companion explain the longer dimming cycle. Together, these mechanisms paint a richer picture of why Orion's giant star fades and brightens.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

#668. Shari Rosenblum, Disney TV Studios’ PR Lead, Exits the Company

The senior vice president of publicity has been with Disney since it purchased Twentieth Century Fox.

Shari Rosenblum has exited Disney after six years with the company, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. Rosenblum accepted a voluntary buyout package — Disney has been offering eligible executives a VERO (Voluntary Early Retirement Offer).

Rosenblum had been senior vice president of communications and publicity at Disney’s TV studios. She came over with Twentieth Century Fox Television in 2019 (Rosenblum had been with the Fox TV studio since 2005). Rosenblum led campaigns for series like Modern Family, Homeland and The Dropout. She is an alum of the University of Arizona and Boston University. Disney has undergone massive layoffs lately. CEO Josh D’Amaro cut hundreds of jobs in September. The latest round follows a staff reduction in July and a large layoff in April. There have been even larger cuts in recent years.

“I’m moving on from my Disney-Fox career with nothing but extreme gratitude.” Rosenblum said. “I’m grateful to Dana [Walden] and Gary [Newman] for taking a chance on an ambitious young publicist over two decades ago, and to the many mentors and champions I’ve had along the way, including Shannon Ryan and Candice Ashton. It’s been a privilege to tell stories for our industry’s top storytellers, especially during this last stretch, with Karey Burke and the incredible executives at 20th TV. I feel beyond fortunate to have worked alongside the most talented and brilliant minds in our industry, and have a deep appreciation for the business of television, the people in it, the shows they make, and the journalists who report on it all.”

“Shari has led PR for Disney Television Studios’ 20th Television and 20th Television Animation with equal parts brilliance and grace,” Ashton said, in part, in an internal email (obtained by THR). “Few people have shaped the voice and reputation of our studio the way she has. Shari is a consummate pro, and an advocate and champion for so many of our teams and creative partners. She has also been a wonderful partner through every curveball along the way, and we’ve shared many laughs together that I will miss very much.”

Rosenblum serves on the Board of P.S. Arts (since 2019), was a member of the Local 600 International Cinematographers & Publicists Guild from 2005-2022, and was a recipient of the Maxwell Weinberg Showmanship Award for Television for her work on Homeland.

#667. Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk have completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station, marking another important step in a major upgrade to the orbiting laboratory's power system. The astronauts finished their work at 3:08 p.m. EDT.

During the spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed a new International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station's 2A electrical power channel. This is the seventh such array added to the station, providing additional electricity for essential operations, including the station's eventual safe and controlled deorbit.

Final Spacewalk Will Complete Solar Array Upgrade

The astronauts also performed several preliminary tasks to prepare for another spacewalk scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 5. During that mission, astronauts will install the eighth and final solar array on the station's 3B power channel. NASA plans to begin live coverage at 6:45 a.m., with information on how to watch available through the agency.

Once the final array is installed, the International Space Station's solar power expansion will be complete. Together, the eight new arrays will increase the station's available power by as much as 30%, raising its electricity generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.

The completed mission, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, marked Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. It was also the 285th spacewalk conducted to support the assembly, maintenance, and improvement of the International Space Station.

If you liked Starship in LEO (low Earth orbit), you're going to love Starship in the new FTO (final tanking orbit).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Artemis IV moon mission will be a complicated affair — especially if SpaceX's Starship ends up being the lunar lander.

For all of the changing components of the Artemis program over the past several years, one of its most persistent may be the question of how many refueling flights Starship will need to land astronauts on the moon.

By summer 2021, it was common knowledge that Starship would require multiple launches to pull off an Artemis moon landing. A Government Accountability Office audit at the time, for example, estimated that it could take up to 16.

Earlier this month, a member of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel said the refueling number could be as high as 22. But that estimate was quickly refuted by SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who posted on his social media platform, X, that it would actually be closer to six or eight.

Perhaps an even bigger head scratcher, though, is how the refueling process will be carried out. Where (and when) will Starship's upper stage gas up when it's off planet? NASA released a graphic during a recent Artemis update that outlined an order of operations for the spacecraft on Artemis IV, which will be the program's first crewed lunar landing.

The mission will launch a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket with the four Artemis IV astronauts aboard NASA's Orion capsule to high Earth orbit, where they will rendezvous and dock with the Starship lunar lander.

Using Starship's engines, the two spacecraft will burn for the moon, and separate upon their arrival in low lunar orbit. Two astronauts will remain aboard Orion, while the other two will head down to the lunar surface in Starship.

After a little run through the regolith and a celebration of America's triumphant return to the moon, the duo will board Starship again to launch back to lunar orbit and dock with Orion before beginning the trip back to Earth.

All that seems well and good for a mission to the moon, and even has some resemblances with missions from NASA's Apollo days. What doesn't seem as immediately obvious when mapping out the Artemis IV mission outline, though, are the steps that Starship will be taking during its refueling process before the astronauts ever make it to space.

Orion will rendezvous with Starship in high Earth orbit — but that's not where the lander will launch initially. According to NASA's Artemis IV outline, SpaceX will first launch a depot ship to low Earth orbit (LEO), which will serve as the repository for all the fuel the Starship lander will eventually need.

The graphic shows a tanker Starship docked with the depot with "(multiple)" written next to it, so we don't know how many refueling flights will be needed for this initial depot fill. Once that's done, SpaceX will launch the Starship lunar lander to join the depot in LEO for its first pit stop.

Then, and this is where some of the head scratching begins, Starship will undock from the depot and raise its altitude to what NASA has labeled the "final tanking orbit," or FTO.

At some point after the Starship lander departs LEO, SpaceX will launch another round of "(multiple)" tanker ships to fill the depot with even more propellant. It will apparently then send the depot to meet the lander for another refill in FTO, where, as the name suggests, the two will dock for the pair's final fuel transfer.

After bidding the depot a second farewell, Starship will ascend to high Earth orbit to meet Orion.

NASA's graphic shows SLS launching Orion before Starship gets the last of its fuel, and the agency's website explainer for Artemis IV says the unusually choreographed order of operations for the mission does serve a purpose.

However many fuel boosts Starship ends up needing to get from LEO to the surface of the moon, its staggered orbital staging will apparently create some flexibility around when SLS can launch the Artemis IV astronauts to begin their mission.

And while Starship's orbital dance seems unnecessarily complicated, NASA says the new approach will actually reduce the amount of fuel SpaceX needs for the mission.

That's partly because Starship will take Orion directly to low lunar orbit, instead of the much higher orbit envisioned in previous mission plans.

But keep in mind: None of this is set in stone. If SpaceX can't demonstrate that its orbital refueling strategy works, or if it can't pull off an uncrewed lunar landing mission by the end of next year, NASA could still select Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander for Artemis IV — assuming Blue Moon is able to check its required boxes in time. Regardless of which company's lander delivers the first Artemis astronauts to the moon's surface, exactly how the pieces of those missions will come together should become clearer as the launch date gets closer. So, while SpaceX's refueling remains an open one for the time being, it's one of many for which we'll soon have an answer.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. #665. Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion and Italy's first since 1953 when he finished third in Sunday's thrilling and crash-hit Mexico City Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

#664. Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang

New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.

Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.

What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.

"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.

"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.

Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.

"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."

How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe

RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.

Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.

The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.

Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.

One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.

Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.

If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.

Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.

"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."

For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.

Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.

These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.

Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.

The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.

Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?

After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.

Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.

These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?

Scientists needed a more definitive sign.

"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.

To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.

An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.

"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.

The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.

"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."

Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.

Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression

To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.

"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.

"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."

Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.

"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."

The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).

The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.

Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.

Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.

Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies

Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.

That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.

The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.

However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.

"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."

While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.

By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.

"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.

New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter

Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.

During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.

These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.

Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.

The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.

The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

#663. Jimmy Kimmel, Seth Meyers Call Out Trump’s “I Wasn’t on the Ballot” Excuse for Midterm Losses: “Shut Up”

The ABC late night host again took aim at the president and urged him to resign after major Republican losses across the country.

Jimmy Kimmel was quick to take aim at Donald Trump on election night after the 2026 midterms saw significant wins by Democrats across the country.

But he wasn’t done. On Wednesday night’s episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, after more results came in and explanations and excuses started streaming in for the blue wave and GOP defeat, the host had more choice words for the president.

Kimmel in particular focused on how Trump claimed, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Related Stories Movies 'The Fight to Fight' Doc, Criticizing Hegseth's Scrutiny of Women in Combat, Sets Release (Exclusive) Midterms 2026 Six Hollywood Consequences of Tuesday's Democratic Blockbuster

“Oh, shut up. Just shut up. Please. Give us a break for one day and shut that ridiculous mouth,” Kimmel said. “You are such a spoiled child. Did you ever learn anything? About manners — or sportsmanship — or simple common decency? Nothing is ever your fault!”

Kimmel added, “You were on the ballot. You’re like dog hair. You’re on everything. You’ve infected every nook and cranny of our lives.”

Indeed, Trump spent months saying he was on the ballot, or told voters to pretend he was, with The Washington Post finding that he made that declaration at least 63 times before Election Day.

Kimmel wasn’t the only late night host to take issue with Trump’s “I wasn’t on the ballot” about-face.

On NBC’s Late Night, Seth Meyers aired a compilation of the multiple times Trump insisted he was essentially on the ballot in the run-up to the midterms.

“I hate to be the one to tell you this, but you were on the fucking ballot, my man,” Meyers said. “Your name might not have been there, but it’s not like everyone forgot who was president. You did like 30 rallies in the month leading up to the midterms. You wouldn’t shut up. You kept talking about how good senators’ asses were. You made the whole thing about you.”

And even if Trump hadn’t suggested that he was on the ballot, the president endorsed many of the Republicans who lost, Kimmel pointed out.

“All your big handpicked candidates lost! You picked Darline Graham to run in South Carolina; you ran Thom Tillis out of the Senate; you backed that pathetic Ken Paxton in Texas; you went all in on Vivek Ramaswamy, and his disgusting campaign ad; and if you hadn’t picked Mr. Charisma J.D. Vance to be your vice president, Republicans would still have that Senate seat they lost in Ohio last night,” Kimmel said.

Kimmel also took issue with Trump, after “whining about election fraud,” telling The New York Times that he would accept the results.

“How is this even news? You’ll accept the results? Oh, thank you,” he said. “How gracious. Results are not for you to accept or reject — they are results. Like, could you imagine this? ‘Spurs say they will accept loss to Knicks in NBA Finals’ No! They don’t have to accept it! It’s the score!”

Kimmel went on to insist that Trump resign.

“Quit already. Just quit,” he said. “Nobody wants you. Even you don’t want to be president anymore. Take that billion dollars’ worth of crypto, buy an island — maybe [Jeffrey] Epstein’s island! Wouldn’t that be a perfect end to this story?”

And the host indicated he was optimistic that a Vance presidency wouldn’t be that bad.

“And maybe you’re thinking, ‘Well, if he quit, wouldn’t that make J.D. Vance president?’ Well, yes, it would. But here’s the thing about J.D. Vance: A person who flipped from ‘Donald Trump is the American Hitler’ to ‘Donald Trump is the greatest president of my generation’ can flip back. It’s easy when you have no spine. He’s a very good flipper.”

On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament.

Unfortunately for Laika, this mission was a one-way trip. The Soviets didn't design a way to bring her back down to Earth. With only 7 days worth of oxygen and a little bit of food on board, Laika launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan with a Russian Sputnik rocket. This was the same kind of rocket used to launch the first Sputnik satellite.

Laika was alive when she reached orbit, but she died shortly afterward because the spacecraft's heat shield had broken off. Laika overheated before she had the chance to die of starvation of oxygen deprivation.

Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. And even nearly 70 years after this flight, it is so heartbreaking to think of Laika on that frightening journey from which she never returned.

Laika was one of many different animals that were used in early spaceflight testing. Both the U.S. and Russia launched a number of primates on flights testing early flight technology. Sadly, like Laika, many of these brave creatures did not make it back.

Unbelievably, though, some did survive the journey. For example, the chimpanzee named Ham and nicknamed the "astrochimp" survived a 1961 test flight to space. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return.
