A tiny robot cube is zipping around the International Space Station, trying to help astronauts with the endless challenging tasks onboard.

Reminiscent of Rocky rolling around the lab helping out Dr. Ryland Grace in Project Hail Mary, the Astrobee robot is a helpful assistant for astronauts aboard the space station.

A metal cube about the size of a toaster, the Astrobees are free-flying robotic assistants that NASA developed to help out astronauts. The first two Astrobee robots (named Bumble and Honey) were sent to the station in 2019. The third Astrobee robot, named Queen, joined later that year, and 7 years later, the program is still going strong.

So what can a free-floating cube help with? The robots are designed to assist the astronauts onboard with testing new technologies in microgravity and helping mission team members back on Earth to better observe inside the station. The little robot cubes can even help astronauts with everyday chores in space.

In this image, snapped by NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins, we can see one of the Astrobee robots helping out in the station's Kibo laboratory.

The idea of a robot assistant helping out with chores and technology development aboard an orbiting space laboratory sounds positively science fiction.

While Astrobee is certainly not the first robot in space or aboard the space station, its compact shape and ability to fly autonomously gives it a unique quality. It really looks like a companion aboard the space station.

While the robotic space helpers of today might be cute little cubes, the success of the Astrobee program begs the question of how robots in space might continue to evolve. Will astronauts on the moon have robotic companions autonomously exploring and helping out? What will they look like?

#660. Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule

Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.

Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor

Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.

The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.

Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.

A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips

The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.

At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.

When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.

This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.

How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin

The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.

The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.

But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.

Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect

To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.

Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.

The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.

"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.

The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.

International Collaboration Solves the Mystery

The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.

Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.

This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.

"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.

The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.

Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.

"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.

The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).

Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

#659. ‘SNL’ Writer Jimmy Fowlie Pays Tribute to Sister Christina Downer After Police Arrest Two for Her Murder

"It brings our family and her friends some relief to know that charges have been filed in connection with Christina’s death... Today I want to spend a little time remembering how much fun I had with her and how lucky I am that she was my sister," Fowlie wrote in a post for Downer's birthday.

Saturday Night Live writer Jimmy Fowlie is paying tribute to his sister, Christina Downer, on her birthday almost a week after police announced they have arrested two people for her murder.

Fowlie shared an Instagram post of himself and Downer at a movie theater in front of a promotional photo-op for Tron: Ares, which he noted was a “video of what turned out to be our last moment together.” He also thanked “everyone who’s reached out” and addressed news that Downer’s boyfriend, Delorean Bijon Brandon, and Kaylee Nicole Markowski had been charged with her murder. Related Stories TV 'SNL': Inde Navarrette Digs at Shane Gillis' Joke About Women Dressing Like "Whores" at the Gym as Tom Hanks Crashes Cold Open News LAPD Arrests Two for Murder of Christina Downer, Sister to 'SNL' Writer Jimmy Fowlie

“It brings our family and her friends some relief to know that charges have been filed in connection with Christina’s death. Because this whole experience has been so endlessly depressing, today I want to spend a little time remembering how much fun I had with her and how lucky I am that she was my sister,” he wrote at the end of the post. “Happy birthday, Chris!”

The Los Angeles Police Department announced on Oct. 30 that Brandon and Markowski had been arrested exactly on Oct. 29. “On December 18, 2025, Christina Downer was reported missing after her ex-husband requested a welfare check when he had not heard from her for an extended period of time. Downer’s boyfriend, Delorean Brandon, claimed that she had moved out several months earlier, leaving behind all her belongings, including her vehicle and dog,” the LAPD said in a statement.

In their statement, police said, “Robbery-Homicide Division detectives assumed the investigation after Downer’s cellphone was discovered washed ashore on Santa Monica Beach. Through various investigative techniques, detectives identified Delorean Brandon and Kaylee Markowski as the individuals responsible for Downer’s murder, the disposal of her body, and the concealment of their involvement.”

Elswhere in Fowlie’s tribute, he described the events that led up to he and Downer’s night at the movies captured in his Instagram video.

“It truly was just an inconsequential night at the movies. I’ve always thought those little photo ops at the Grove were so puzzling. I’d see them and try to imagine a world where me and my friends would pose in front of one non-ironically. For some reason on this day, i decided to make @nletreize take one of me and Christina as we were leaving,” he wrote. I just wanted to be extra and make her laugh, and I love how you can see her giggling as she walks up. She’s wearing her slippers which i think is so cute. In this video i feel like you can feel how sweet her energy is.”

The SNL writer continued, “She was one of my favorite people to make laugh. You could argue my whole comedy career was actually born out of sitting at the dinner table as kids and acting dumb while our dad became increasingly irate at me. It was a sacrifice that was always worth it.”

On Dec. 22, 2025, Fowlie shared a social media post asking for help finding his missing sister, sharing a multiple of images of Downer. Months later, in April of this year, he announced that “the LAPD has informed our family that Christina is no longer alive, and the case has officially transitioned from a missing person to a homicide investigation.”

The LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division will present the case to the L.A. Country District Attorney’s Office for filing consideration. The investigation is still ongoing.

On Aug. 2, 2027, the moon's shadow will sweep across Tunisia, giving Star Wars fans a rare chance to experience a total solar eclipse at the real-life filming locations of Tatooine.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Aug. 2, 2027, the moon's shadow will sweep across some of the most iconic filming locations from Star Wars, plunging them into darkness during what's being called the "eclipse of the century".

The path of the 2027 total solar eclipse will cross southern Tunisia, where several locations were used to bring the fictional desert planet Tatooine to life. From the dunes of Mos Espa to the rocky Jundland Wastes, Star Wars fans will have the rare opportunity to experience totality at the very places where their favorite scenes were filmed

But not every famous filming location will experience totality, so choosing where to watch will be crucial. Here are four locations that fall directly in the moon's shadow. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Location: south of Chott el-Gharsa, Tozeur Governorate, southwest Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 9 seconds

With a massive budget and three prequels to make, Lucasfilm built a new film set that would double as the Mos Espa spaceport on Tatooine for The Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones. This is where Qui-Gon Jinn, Obi-Wan Kenobi, Jar Jar Binks and Padme get stranded, where they meet Anakin Skywalker and where the podrace takes place. Now abandoned, it's in the middle of nowhere, between two huge salt lakes and subject to the intense heat and moving Eriguet dunes — but it is firmly within the path of totality. Nearby are two other shooting locations — the Ong Jemel outcrop, where Darth Maul arrives on the scene, and Yardang, where Qui-Gon and Darth Maul battle — the first-ever lightsaber duel filmed on location.

Location: Jebel Sidi Bouhlel canyon, Dghoumès National Park, Tozeur, southwest Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 37 seconds

Often called "Star Wars Canyon" by fans and crew, Maguer Gorge in Jebel Sidi Bouhlel doubled as the Jundland Wastes of Tatooine in Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope. It's where Luke Skywalker is attacked by Tusken Raiders, where Obi-Wan Kenobi first appears and where Luke and Obi-Wan discover the slaughtered Jawas. The canyon also provided the distant view of Mos Eisley — the famous "wretched hive of scum and villainy." On Aug. 2, 2027, you'll likely be pointing your macrobinoculars at the eclipsed sun rather than Tusken Raiders.

Steven Spielberg later filmed here for Raiders of the Lost Ark, including the scene in which Indiana Jones threatens to destroy the Ark with a bazooka. Just south of Dghoumès National Park is a desert oasis called Bouhlel Sdada, used for the archaeological dig scenes in Raiders.

Location: Ajim city center, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:10 a.m. CET; 3 minutes, 55 seconds

Djerba Island's palm trees, beaches and Mediterranean horizons will make it a popular destination for eclipse chasers after a long totality away from the heat and crowds of Luxor in Egypt. It's also home to three notable Star Wars filming locations. The original movie's Mos Eisley footage was shot here, with Ajim doubling as a Stormtrooper checkpoint ("These are not the droids you're looking for"), the Cantina exterior, and an alley near Docking Bay 94 where stormtroopers watch the Millennium Falcon blast off. In reality, it's an abandoned bakery.

Location: Ajim outskirts, Médenine Governorate, Djerba island, Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes

Just north of Ajim, this mosque — originally a fisherman's house — was used as a stand-in for "Old Ben's" house, where Obi-Wan Kenobi gives Luke Skywalker a lightsaber. It was used purely for photography, and no actors set foot here. It was also cut from the movie's Special Edition in 1997, so you'll only find it in the original version. Completists might also want to check out Sidi Jemour Mosque to the north, which was used for scenes with Biggs Darklighter that didn't even make the final cut. IYKYK …

Tunisia's Star Wars locations are spread across the south, so the easiest way to see several is on an organized tour or with a private driver and guide. Tozeur is the main base for visiting Mos Espa, Ong Jemel and Jebel Sidi Bouhlel, with local operators offering half-day and full-day 4x4 excursions into the desert. Djerba Island is the other major hub for three sights. Longer multi-day tours typically connect Tozeur with Matmata, home to Hotel Sidi Idriss — the Lars Homestead — as well as Djerba.

One tour company, Star Wars Tours, is running a (sold-out) special departure called "Eclipse tour from the Outer Rim" that witnesses totality at the Mos Espa set. Other Star Wars-focused tour operators include Galaxy Tours, though one-day trips to the Mos Espa set from Tozeur are also available.

Tunisia is surely one of the most attractive destinations for the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse. Historical cloud cover is exceptionally low, while totality reaches around five and a half minutes near the centerline. It also offers established tourism infrastructure and generally lower August temperatures than Egypt, making it an obvious alternative for eclipse chasers hoping to avoid the biggest crowds around Luxor.

You can, of course, visit the Star Wars sets in the days before or after the eclipse. For Tunisia's maximum duration of totality, consider Sfax, where darkness lasts 5 minutes, 41 seconds, or nearby Chaffar Beach, with its long, open Mediterranean coastline. Offshore, the low-lying Kerkennah Islands get around 5 minutes, 39 seconds. Inland, Sidi Bouzid offers about 5 minutes, 33 seconds beneath typically dry skies, while the spectacular Roman amphitheater at El Jem gets 4 minutes, 23 seconds. On Djerba Island, meanwhile, beaches and extensive resort infrastructure make combining an eclipse chase with a conventional Mediterranean vacation particularly easy — with a view of Mos Eisley thrown in for good measure.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#657. Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves

Trees have a remarkable ability to sense their own shape and adjust their growth to stay upright. This awareness of body position, known as proprioception, was once thought to exist only in animals. However, in 2012, researchers working with INRAE demonstrated that plants also possess this ability (Bastien R. et al., PNAS).

This internal sense allows plants to monitor their posture and make adjustments that help them grow as straight as possible (Moulia et al., Science). Although scientists had established that plants could detect their own shape, the biological processes responsible for turning that information into physical movement remained a mystery.

How Scientists Isolated Trees' Hidden Sense

Plants use several kinds of information to guide their growth. They respond to gravity, detect the direction of sunlight, and monitor the shape and position of their own stems. To understand how this internal sense works independently, researchers needed to eliminate the directional signals provided by gravity and light.

They developed an unusual experimental system designed to isolate proprioception. Young trees were placed on a horizontal platform that rotated around its axis inside a sphere illuminated equally from every direction. The rotating platform prevented the trees from receiving a consistent directional signal from gravity, while the surrounding light eliminated cues about which way they should grow.

This arrangement allowed the researchers to investigate how trees respond to their own shape without relying on the usual environmental signals that influence their growth.

The Muscle-Like Wood That Helps Trees Straighten Themselves

The experiment began with young poplar trees positioned horizontally. As the trees grew, their stems gradually curved upward, bringing their tops back toward a vertical position.

This response depends on a specialized type of wood called tension wood. Unlike ordinary wood, tension wood can generate pulling forces as it develops. When it forms along the upper side of a stem, it acts much like a contracting muscle, pulling the stem upward and causing it to bend.

After approximately ten days, once the trees had developed a noticeable curve, researchers moved them into the experimental apparatus. Over the following weeks, something remarkable happened. Instead of maintaining their curved shapes, the stems slowly straightened until they became nearly straight again.

To determine what caused this change, the team examined the structure of the wood that developed during the straightening process.

They found that the original tension wood, which had formed along the upper side of the stems and pulled them upward, stopped developing once the experimental system was activated. At the same time, identical tension wood began forming on the opposite side.

This newly formed wood appeared to act like an opposing muscle, producing a pulling force in the other direction. As the forces worked against each other, the curved stems gradually returned to a straight shape.

The production of tension wood involves a complex sequence of biological events controlled at the cellular level. The findings indicate that a tree's internal sense of its own shape helps regulate this process, determining where tension wood develops to correct its posture.

A Surprising Discovery About How Trees Control Their Shape

Previously, scientists believed that tension wood formed only on the upper side of stems, where it helped pull them upward. This is particularly noticeable near the bases of trees growing on mountain slopes, where trunks often need to curve to maintain an upright position.

The new research reveals that tension wood has a more versatile role. It can develop on opposing sides of a stem and generate forces in different directions, functioning much like the opposing muscle groups animals use to maintain posture and control movement.

This discovery suggests that trees possess a sophisticated system for coordinating their growth. They combine information about their surroundings (such as light and gravity) with an internal awareness of their own shape. By processing these signals, they can regulate where tension wood develops and adjust their posture accordingly.

Why This Discovery Matters for Forests and Agriculture

The ability to sense and correct their own shape is especially important when trees encounter environmental disturbances. Powerful storms, landslides, and other extreme events can bend or displace trees, making the capacity to regain an appropriate posture essential for their resilience.

Understanding this mechanism could become increasingly valuable as climate change exposes forests to more extreme conditions.

The findings also have practical implications for forestry and agriculture. By identifying plants with particularly effective proprioception, scientists may be able to select varieties that grow straighter, maintain better posture, and produce higher-quality wood.

In agriculture, the same knowledge could help researchers develop cereal crops that are less likely to fall over before harvest. This problem, known as lodging, can cause significant yield losses when crops collapse toward the end of the growing season.

The discovery could also improve timber quality. Poorly coordinated tension wood formation can create excessive internal stresses in trees, potentially affecting the properties of the wood they produce.

Bruno Moulia, INRAE research director, explained:

"What we have uncovered is a genuine sensorimotor loop operating in the woody parts of trees! Poor coordination in the successive activation of tension wood results in excessive internal tension, which can affect wood quality. These findings therefore reshape more applied research aimed at improving wood quality... and at obtaining trees that are as straight and as relaxed as possible, whatever life throws at them!"

The research also highlights the importance of combining expertise from different scientific fields to understand the complex ways plants interact with their environment.

Félix Hartman, INRAE research engineer, emphasized the collaborative effort behind the discovery:

"Revealing the remarkable capabilities of trees requires a great deal of ingenuity. In this project, we achieved it by bringing together researchers from different disciplines, with complementary skills and perspectives. This requires time and perseverance, but these interdisciplinary discoveries show that the effort is worthwhile."

Materials provided by INRAE - National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and Environment. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.

The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats.

The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old, Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old. That means it is still host to collisions between planetary bodies similar to the ones that rocked the solar system during its infancy.

The team behind this research gained new insights into the Cat's Tail using 14 years of observations. This allowed them to solve the long-standing mystery of the violent conditions under which it formed.

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies — think something like Pluto," team leader Arin Avsar of the University of Arizona said in a statement. "Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

Comparing Beta Pictoris and our solar system, one thing rapidly becomes apparent: our cosmic neighborhood is relatively well-ordered. The planets orbit the sun with most space rocks neatly delegated into bands: the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the Kuiper belt out beyond the orbit of Neptune.

However, this is a stark contrast to the solar system's violent and chaotic youth. Back then, the solar system was host to an infant star surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust in which collisions between bodies called planetesimals — the building blocks of planets — were commonplace.

Astronomers can't look back to the solar system's infancy, so to learn more about how our cosmic backyard took shape, they study nearby young planetary systems. Systems like Beta Pictoris. That doesn't mean it has been quick to divulge its secrets, though.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

This new study revealed that the feline feature is cat-like in more ways than just its shape. It's also pleasingly fluffy, Hubble observations suggest. That's because the grains that compose it are extremely porous.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," team member Kevin Wagner of the U of A said.

The scientists also discovered a hitherto undiscovered feature in the Cat's Tail — a warp that seems to be the result of an interaction between the trail of material and one of the planets in the system, Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant planet 10 times more massive than Jupiter.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament to how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units [one astronomical unit being the distance between Earth and the sun]."

The team's research was published last month in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #655. Matt Damon Reveals Why He Passed on Starring in ‘Ted’

'The Odyssey' star would've played John Bennett, a role that went to fellow Boston native Mark Wahlberg.

In a new interview with GQ, Damon revealed that he passed on starring in Seth MacFarlane‘s 2012 comedy as John Bennett, the best friend of the foul-mouthed, party-loving teddy bear named Ted.

“I don’t want to live with the regret, but I can tell you that I passed on Ted, and I’ve never had this experience where I laughed so hard reading a script,” The Odyssey star said. “I literally took it to dinner and was reading parts of it out to my friends at dinner. And then I just got too clever by half. I don’t know what I was thinking. I was like, Well, maybe the teddy bear’s actually the best part.…” Related Stories Movies Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Will Return to Theaters Next Month as Awards Season Heats Up Lifestyle GQ Expands Men of the Year Footprint in L.A.

Damon went on to explain why he decided to go in a different direction — and why he still thinks about what could have been.

“I overthought it and I talked myself out of it,” he said. “And because it shot in Boston, it would’ve been a chance for me to be home — my father’s passed away now, and I look back and I go, Man, that would’ve been six months back [home].”

The role ultimately went to fellow Boston native Mark Wahlberg, who stars alongside the talking teddy bear in the 2015 sequel, Ted 2.

Damon praised Wahlberg’s performance, saying the “right actor” got the part and that the movie turned out great. “I wouldn’t have made it any better,” he added.

The success of the two films later spawned a Ted prequel series on Peacock, which ran for two seasons.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter earlier this year, the Family Guy creator discussed the franchise’s future after the series ended and said he would be interested in making a third film.

“It’s up to Universal. It’s up to Peacock. A third season in the near future — I don’t know that there are any plans for that,” he said. “I’ve thrown the idea out that maybe we do a direct-to-Peacock Ted feature with this cast. That might be something that’s kind of fun. It was what, 10 years between the last Ted movie and the first episode of this series, and people were still there for it. He’s a character we can bring back at any time.”

#653. Merz says next German president 'must be a woman' — report

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second term is due to end in March next year. Meanwhile, Merz has called for 'digital sovereignty' in the era of AI.

This blog is now closed. It was a round-up of some of the top headlines from and about Germany on November 2, 2026:

We're closing the blog today. Thank you for reading, we'll be back tomorrow again!

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out in favor of having a woman succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president.

"I will propose a consensus candidate to the party, a candidate from the political center," Merz said at a non-public meeting of local Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chairs in Berlin, participants told the German DPA news agency.

"I am firm in my belief that it must be a woman," he reportedly added.

Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government.

Current incumbent Steinmeier, a former Social Democrat (SPD) foreign minister, became president in 2017 and his second term will end in March 2027.

Bavarian premier Markus Söder recently proposed Ilse Aigner from his Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's Bavarian sister party.

But the CDU itself may propose an alternative candidate from within its own ranks, with current parliamentary speaker Julia Klöckner, Families Minister Karin Prien and former CDU leader and Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer all having been mentioned.

The CDU's top leadership is expected to propose a candidate on November 9.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Germany must speed up its development of artificial intelligence capabilities to protect its "digital sovereignty" in an era of rapid change.

Speaking at a conference on AI in Berlin, the chancellor said countries risked surrendering control to outside providers by failing to keep pace.

"That is why we must, at all costs, avoid becoming entirely dependent on third parties when it comes to developing and using this ​technology," he said. "And that is why the issue of digital sovereignty in the context of ​AI becomes a truly existential question."

Merz stressed that people and their dignity must remain central to political efforts to manage rapid technological progress, saying AI development should be guided by human values.

He also said adapting to AI-driven changes required "an enormous technological and organizational effort, a far-reaching modernization of our state and our economy."

Merz pointed to Germany's strength as a business location and home of industrial engineering. He also said international cooperation was crucial, and that Berlin would seek to work with like-minded partners such as France and Canada to share knowledge and diversify supply chains.

Merz appointed a minister for digitalization and modernization last year after taking office. Although many German companies have adopted and integrated AI technology, critics say Germany has been too slow to build the digital infrastructure and ​skills needed to exploit it fully.

Alexander Zverev officially rose to the No. 1 spot in the men's tennis rankings on Monday, becoming only the second German man to hold the title after Boris Becker 35 years ago.

"Today is a historic day for German tennis," said German Tennis Federation President Dietloff von Arnim. "Sascha has earned this spot at the top of the world rankings through extraordinary perseverance and hard work."

The 29-year-old beat Flavio Cobolli to win the French Open title in June, before going on to lift the US Open trophy after defeating Ben Shelton in September.

He also reached the final at Wimbledon this year, ultimately falling to Jannik Sinner, and the Australian Open semifinals.

He is the 30th male player to reach No. 1, and the oldest in more than 50 years to top the rankings for the first time.

"I had to wait," said Zverev, who reached the top spot more than four years after becoming No. 2. "But sometimes you've got to wait for the best things in life. I'm super happy, super thrilled."

Sinner, who had been holding the No.1 spot since April 13, dropped to second, ahead of Carlos Alcaraz.

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has confirmed that a summit with Russian and American advisers "at the highest possible level" is being planned.

The AfD's foreign policy spokesman, Markus Frohnmaier, said the meeting is likely to take place in Abu Dhabi in early 2027 and will focus on restoring Russian gas deliveries to Germany.

DW understands that AfD leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla would attend the meeting if US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also present.

Such a meeting would represent a major PR coup for the far-right party, which remains shunned by most of Germany's political establishment despite leading national opinion polls.

"The focus here will be on discussions with the American side, as well as the Russian side, particularly with regard to economic partnership, energy partnership and also the Nord Stream question," Frohnmaier told journalists in Berlin.

According to Frohnmaier, Kirill Dmitriev, a special adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, is coordinating with contacts in the US administration.

Dmitriev greeted Witkoff, US President Donald Trump's Middle East envoy, when he arrived in Russia for talks last month.

Dmitriev has also been cultivating contacts in Germany. He and Frohnmaier met at an economic forum in St. Petersburg earlier this year.

In September, Dmitriev described the anti-immigration, anti-EU AfD as "the hope for Germany" during regional election campaigns. The party wants to end sanctions on Russia and halt weapons deliveries to Ukraine.

While the Abu Dhabi summit is expected to focus on business and economic ties, Frohnmaier said such formats can "establish a framework for dialogue" and help "work toward peace."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier attended the opening of a new Jewish Academy in Frankfurt on Monday.

The €40-million ($45-million) educational institution, which was inaugurated under tight security, is to be a "place of dialogue," Steinmeier said.

He denounced antisemitism and said it must be "put in its place, without loopholes or reservations," whether it comes from the left or the right of the political spectrum.

The president also warned against what he described as the increasing political exploitation of hatred toward Jews.

"All parties have a duty to confront antisemitism throughout their entire sphere of influence — from the party leadership down to the rank and file and among their supporters," he said. "Antisemitism must not be allowed to influence government work anywhere in Germany."

The academy's opening ceremony was also attended by the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, who described the center as a "milestone" that would be "dedicated to the full diversity of Jewish thought and Jewish experiences."

He said Jewish life in Germany was under greater threat than at any time since the Holocaust, with an "explosive rise" in antisemitism since the Hamas-led terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

He said the new center could play a role in turning this around, stressing the importance of openness, enlightenment, dialogue and "education, education and yet more education."

The academy is funded by the federal government, the state of Hesse, the city of Frankfurt and the Central Council of Jews.

It is aimed at a wide audience and offers a range of programs and events, including international conferences, educational courses, and panel discussions.

The German Retail Association says society as a whole has a responsibility to prevent the kind of violence that followed youth protests in several German cities on Saturday.

In Frankfurt, rioters threw stones and petrol bombs, smashed shop windows and looted businesses. Violent confrontations were also reported in other parts of the country.

"We must not tolerate a social climate in which retailers cannot always be certain, wherever they are, that they can go about their business unhindered," association boss Stefan Genth said.

"This applies to society as a whole. We are all called upon to act," he said, adding that it must be clear that violence, or the threat of it, has no place in Germany.

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across the country over the weekend calling for better education funding and measures to bring down the cost of living. The protests were largely peaceful, although in some cities they were followed by rioting and looting.

Genth said it was alarming "that some retailers in certain locations felt compelled last Saturday to take extra security measures or, in some cases, to close their shops entirely."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to tell a conference of local party leaders of  his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) that he saw a positive aspect to weekend youth protests, while condemning violence that occurred in their aftermath.

"I take above all a positive message from the weekend: The young generation is politically engaged and is concerned about its future," he is to say, according to a speech released beforehand to news agencies.

In the planned speech, Merz says the government is making efforts not to burden the younger generation with the costs of an aging society.

"That is why we are carrying out pension reform for young people, why we are concerned about our security, and why we are preparing our economy for the digital future," Merz's speech runs.

However, the chancellor has harsh words for those who rioted and attacked police on the sidelines of the mostly peaceful protests.

"Violence has no place on our streets, and my government will show no tolerance in this regard," the speech says.

"Anyone who attacks police officers and emergency service personnel and loots shops is attacking our freedom, mocking society and the legitimate interests of young people," the chancellor emphasizes in the speech.

"The offenders will feel the full force of the law."

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across Germany over the weekend, mostly peacefully.

However, several of the protests were followed by sometimes severe riots, such as in Frankfurt, where stones and petrol bombs were thrown, shop windows were smashed and looting took place.

More than 100 police officers were injured.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The trade union IG Metall, which represents workers in the metalworking, electrical, steel, automotive and industrial manufacturing sectors, has called on thousands of employees to walk out at more than 2,000 workplaces nationwide by the end of the week.

A number of companies are expected to be affected, including carmakers Opel and Rolls-Royce, consumer goods giant Procter & Gamble, e-mobility supplier Vitesco, Daimler Truck AG and precision engineering firm Paul Beier GmbH.

The union, Germany and Europe's largest, is calling for a 5% pay rise over a 12-month period, along with job and site security.

Employers have put forward an offer of a one-off payment next year and a pay rise of 1.3% in July 2028, citing Germany's economic woes and cost pressures on industry to justify not meeting the union's demand.

Education Minister Karin Prien has said the violence that occurred in the aftermath of youth protests on Saturday evening was in part an indication that the integration of people of migrant background into German society could be improved.

Prien told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk said that the "for the most part peaceful demonstrations" had been followed by rioting by left-wing radicals "but also by others who probably come from migrant milieus."

She said that recognizing this fact was not about stirring up resentments, which she called "politically wrong," but about facing reality and getting a picture of why people resort to such means.

"And if they come from migrant milieus, we should be worried about it and look at the causes," said Prien, a member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

She said one question was why integration succeeds less well in some groups than in others.

"And it's not about the question of a passport. It's about the question: Why have people not been integrated into our society and what can be done so it works better in future," she said.

Her comments came despite the fact that authorities in Frankfurt, which saw the worst of the violence, said that most of the people they arrested in connection with rioting over the weekend were German citizens.

Prien's remarks came after archconservative Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) said the "peaceful demonstrations were hijacked toward the evening by violence-prone left-wing groups and migrant anarchists," without offering evidence for who was behind the violent turn in the demonstrations.

Dobrindt's comment was, however, called into question by Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's federal coalition government.

"What are migrant groups, then? Are these people living in Germany in the third generation who are German nationals? Where do we stop differentiating here? I think this is going in the wrong direction," he said.

Pistorius said, however, that whoever had been responsible for the rioting had to be punished for it.

His intervention comes as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues, without evidence, to blame migration for most of the country's problems, with Dobrindt seeming to adopt some of the populist party's anti-migrant rhetoric.

A 34-year-old man accused of having killed two people while racing with his car through a pedestrian zone in the eastern city of Leipzig in May is going on trial on Monday.

The accused has also been charged with 85 counts of attempted murder.

State prosecutors argue that the man planned the attack with the intent of killing people with his car, which reached speeds of up to 90 kmh (56 mph) during the rampage.

A 63-year-old woman and a 77-year-old man were killed in the incident.

The accused is said to have checked into a psychiatric clinic of his own free will a month before the attack and to have been discharged at his own wish a few days prior to it.

However, a psychiatric assessment has found no indications of diminished capacity on his part.

The trial has been scheduled to last until July of next year.

German natural gas storage facilities are currently only around 61.2% full, according to figures from a European platform that monitors storage levels. AGSI.

That falls well short of the 70% targeted by Sunday.

However, a spokeswoman for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said there was no cause for concern.

"Germany's gas supply is secure for the coming winter, even with the current storage levels," she said.

"Based on the current assessment, we expect Germany to get through the winter in good shape. Security of supply depends not only on storage levels, but also on actual gas withdrawals, ongoing gas imports and additional precautionary measures," the spokeswoman said.

But Sebastian Heinermann,  Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of the Initiative Energien Speichern (Energy Storage Initiative), a mouthpiece for the sector, said the current storage levels were a "serious warning."     "Germany is entering the heating season with smaller safety reserves. This increases the vulnerability of the gas supply, particularly in the event of exceptionally low temperatures or additional disruptions to gas imports," Heinermann said.

The Economy Ministry has said the war in Iran, which has brought a partial blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital transport route for global gas and oil, was one factor behind the current low storage level.

However, it says Germany now has more options to access additional gas than was the case in 2022, when the gas supply from Russia was cut off amid Moscow's launch of its invasion of Ukraine.

The German and British defense ministers are also expected to focus on artificial intelligence as a field for enhanced military cooperation at talks on Monday.

"By jointly testing, developing and, finally, introducing AI in our armed forces, we want to deepen our cooperation and keep pace with those who want to hurt us," UK Defense Minister Wes Streeting wrote in the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung ahead of talks with his German counterpart, Boris Pistorius.

"Our opponents' readiness to harm us is not new. What is new is their abilities to do so. This demands an answer from all of us in Europe," he wrote.

Representatives from government and industry from both countries are to meet in the spring of next year to push ahead with the implementation of these plans, he wrote.

Two years ago, Germany and the United Kingdom agreed to cooperate more closely on military matters in the so-called Trinity House Agreement.

A year later, both countries announced that they would be focusing more on cyber defense as part of this cooperation.

A two-day conference in Berlin that will look at ways of enhancing Germany's digital infrastructure, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), is to be opened by the minister for digital affairs, Karsten Wildberger, on Monday morning.

More than 1,000 guests, including digital ministers from Europe and Canada, are expected to attend the summit, which this year will focus largely on the uses and safety of AI and new developments in the field.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is scheduled to hold a speech in the afternoon and to meet with a robot from the German company Neura Robotics.

The company develops robots that can see, hear and feel and are potentially utilizable in both industries and households.

The event is being held for the 19th time since its inception in 2006 as the National IT Summit. It did not take place in 2021, an election year in Germany.

Guten Morgen from DW's newsroom in Bonn as the first, chilly week of November gets underway.

That wintry cold makes a report that gas storage levels are well below what they should be at the start of the heating season sobering reading.

Meanwhile, an annual digital summit in Berlin that will look at ways of boosting the field of artificial intelligence (AI) in Germany and Europe is also kicking off.

It is set to bring a hopefully friendly encounter between Chancellor Merz and a humanoid robot from the German company Neura Robotics.

AI will also be on the agenda at afternoon talks between Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and his UK counterpart Wes Streeting, as the two discuss enhancing German-British military cooperation.

#652. Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer

Scientists at the University of Virginia Comprehensive Cancer Center have developed a promising experimental strategy for treating glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. The new approach could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles that have limited the effectiveness of existing brain cancer treatments.

The research team, led by UVA's Roger Abounader, MD, PhD, identified tiny genetic molecules known as "microRNAs" that can interfere with several genes responsible for the development and growth of glioblastoma. To deliver these molecules into the brain, the researchers combined specialized nanoparticles, focused ultrasound and microscopic bubbles. Together, these technologies offer a way to temporarily cross the brain's protective barrier, which normally prevents many treatments from reaching brain tumors and other neurological conditions.

"This new approach could help target numerous molecules that promote cancer growth, including those for which no drugs exist, at the same time to achieve better therapies," said Abounader, a professor at UVA's School of Medicine in the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Cancer Biology, as well as its Comprehensive Cancer Center and Center for RNA Science and Medicine. "We are hoping to translate our findings into future clinical trials for patients with glioblastoma and other brain tumors."

Why Glioblastoma Is So Difficult to Treat

Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. It claims more than 13,000 lives in the United States each year. One reason it is so difficult to treat is that cancer cells spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it nearly impossible for surgeons to remove the entire tumor.

Another major challenge is the brain's natural "blood-brain barrier." This protective system helps shield the brain from harmful substances, including toxins and infectious agents. Unfortunately, it also blocks many drugs that could otherwise be used to attack brain cancer.

Current treatment generally begins with surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Patients then receive radiation therapy and chemotherapy to help control the remaining cancer and extend survival. Despite these efforts, glioblastoma remains exceptionally difficult to manage.

The UVA researchers are pursuing a different strategy. Instead of relying on drugs that target individual cancer-related processes, their approach uses microRNAs, small pieces of genetic material capable of suppressing the activity of multiple problematic genes at the same time.

By disrupting several genes that help glioblastoma grow and survive, the treatment could potentially slow or even stop tumor growth. This ability to target multiple cancer-driving mechanisms is especially important because combining several conventional cancer drugs can produce harmful side effects. In addition, many of the molecules involved in cancer growth cannot currently be targeted by available medications.

Using Ultrasound to Deliver Cancer-Fighting Molecules

Getting these genetic molecules into the brain presents another major challenge. To overcome it, Abounader's team uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing researchers to direct sound waves precisely toward the intended area.

The ultrasound works with tiny "microbubbles" to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier. This creates a brief opportunity for nanoparticles carrying the microRNAs to pass through the barrier and enter the brain, where they can act on genes involved in tumor growth.

The researchers tested this approach in laboratory experiments and animal models of glioblastoma. Their findings showed that the microRNA treatment slowed tumor growth and helped the animals survive longer.

Although these results are encouraging, the strategy remains experimental and will require additional research before it can be evaluated in human patients. Abounader believes the findings provide an important early indication that the technology could eventually benefit people with glioblastoma and potentially those with other types of cancer.

"This approach could have broad applications for several brain and other human diseases," Abounader said. "We and many others are intensively working to lighten the burden of cancer, and hopefully also completely cure it, but this requires a continued investment in cancer and medical research."

UVA Expands Focused Ultrasound Cancer Research

UVA Health has been at the forefront of focused ultrasound research since the technology's early development. Over the years, its scientists have built an extensive research program investigating how precisely directed sound waves might be used to treat a wide range of medical conditions.

Recognizing the technology's potential in cancer care, UVA partnered with the Charlottesville-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation to establish the Focused Ultrasound Immuno-Oncology (FUSION) Center. It is the first center in the world devoted specifically to investigating how focused ultrasound can be combined with cancer immunotherapy. Researchers believe this combination could lead to major advances in cancer treatment during the 21st century.

The effort also supports the broader missions of UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center and UVA's Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology, both of which are working to improve care through new medical discoveries.

UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center is among just 57 cancer centers nationwide to receive the National Cancer Institute's prestigious "comprehensive" designation. The recognition reflects its excellence in cancer research and patient care.

The Manning Institute was established to speed the discovery and development of new medicines and potential cures for some of the most difficult diseases. Its work is supported by a statewide clinical trials network designed to make emerging treatments more accessible to patients as they move through research and testing.

Abounader and his colleagues published their experimental approach and initial laboratory findings in JCI, the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The study is open access and can be read free of charge.

The research team included Shekhar Saha, Ying Zhang, Myron K. Gibert Jr., Collin Dube, Farina Hanif, Elizabeth Qian Xu Mulcahy, Sylwia Bednarek, Yunan Sun, Pawel Marcinkiewicz, Xiantao Wang, Gijung Kwak, Ahsan H. Polash, Haolin Li, Kadie Hudson, Manikarna Dinda, Tapas Saha, Matthew McCord, Fadila Guessous, Nichola Cruickshanks, Rossymar Rivera Colon, Lily Dell'Olio, Rajitha Anbu, Wenjie Liu, Songy Choi, Benjamin Kefas, Pankaj Kumar, Alexander L. Klibanov, David Schiff, Jung Soo Suk, Justin Hanes, Jamie Mata, Markus Hafner and Abounader. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Cancer Institute through grants U01 CA220841 and P30 CA044579, along with the NIH's National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke through grants R01 NS122222 and R21 NS122136. Additional support was provided by a UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center pilot grant, a Schiff Foundation grant, the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, and the Focused Ultrasound Foundation.

Materials provided by University of Virginia Health System. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.

Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) smashed into Dimorphos in September 2022, changing the asteroid's orbit in a pioneering planetary defense demonstration. Hera's job is to survey the damage and refine our understanding of the impact, as well as the asteroids themselves.

Hera performed braking maneuvers earlier in October to slow its approach and put it on course to rendezvous with the binary system. The spacecraft is designed to make follow-up observations of the asteroids using 12 payloads, providing new insights that will prove valuable for planetary defense efforts. The mission also carries a pair of cubesats for a closer look and eventual landing on the 495-foot-wide (151 meters) Dimorphos.

For now, Hera is continuing its approach and preparing for arrival, with a big reveal expected to occur later this month.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer," said ESA's mission manager Ian Carnelli. "We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos — the first object in the solar system to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action — on 25 November."

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. The OG sci-fi browser game is still going strong.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you were on the Internet in the early 2000s looking for free browser games to play, OGame was a blooming sci-fi strategy sensation that couldn't be ignored. With online servers providing the structure for a living and evolving universe where players fought, traded, and created empires from scratch, its limited visual presentation was no issue.

Times have changed, but GameForge hasn't gone anywhere. OGame has been ported to mobile devices, and content updates have kept it alive and fresh for much longer than a plethora of installable MMO games.

With the Orion update, which will hit the newly launched universes (servers) on November 6, OGame is introducing conflicts against non-player-character (NPC) enemies, wave-based battles, co-op missions, and completely new systems that can also be disrupted by other players.

The game's endurance and such a major reinvention are stunning achievements, so we asked GameForge's Martin Liedtke (Director, Products of Browser Games) and Enrico Mareth (Senior Project Manager for OGame PC and Mobile) about the many challenges of working on OGame alongside the community for so long, what Orion is bringing to the table, and what's next for this worldwide phenomenon.

Some quotes have been editorialized and lightly trimmed for better flow.

"OGame has an enduring core: You build an interstellar empire, and your decisions matter... Keeping it fresh means adding meaningful choices to that foundation," said Liedtke. "Orion adds missions against automated opponents (PvE) alongside missions open to other players (PvP)... It supports different appetites for risk."

The GameForge veteran noted, however, that it's the community that "supplies another kind of freshness" after the studio releases the new content. "We develop the systems; players create much of the history."

Part of this approach is keeping tabs on how very different kinds of players approach what's available. "Some commanders concentrate on their economy; others enjoy expeditions or carefully coordinated fleet operations... Orion follows that approach; more experienced players can dig into fleet composition, progression, and cooperation. The aim is to offer worthwhile choices."

Liedtke also noted that "OGame's PvP has become a sophisticated contest of information and coordination" over time. Some players like to scout targets and organize combined attacks when enemy fleets are vulnerable. Those battles resolve automatically, but it's the planning that "can be remarkably intricate," especially after so many years of updates.

The PvE in Orion doesn't sacrifice any of those intricacies or density. In fact, it's adding a "more structured layer" that gives players clear objectives. In most cases, they'll have to cooperate to obtain better rewards. "There is a strong case for introducing that kind of cooperative PvE earlier. It gives players another reason to build and use fleets together."

Over two decades later, how people choose to engage with OGame has changed, pushing GameForge to consider supporting new platforms. Today, mobile devices have become essential to free-to-play games' success over time.

Mareth told us their importance "has made touch controls, navigation, and clarity on smaller screens central development considerations," even if thousands of players still remain attached to PC as their main platform. "We're currently working on a design overhaul of the app, combining what we've learned with players' feedback."

Liedtke also said there is more overlap between PC and mobile players than you might imagine.

"The same player might check their empire on a phone and spend a longer session planning in the browser." Liedtke also noted that "Different playstyles also have different needs," adding that activities like mining and trading fit "comfortably" into short mobile sessions, but complex fleet operations benefit from sitting in front of one's PC.

While it's a game of interstellar conflict and sci-fi spaceships, OGame does take a lot of inspiration from real-life science, even if it stretches that science well past its limits. "When ships are destroyed in battle, the debris field can form a moon around a player's planet," explains Liedtke. "The chance (of that happening) is linked to the real lunar cycle: it is higher around a full moon than a new moon."

He noted it's a "playful connection" to astronomy, "rather than a simulation of how real moons form," but the developers thought it was cool to influence the game via things that happen in our own sky.

This possible in-game "event" also led to one of the best examples of player ingenuity in OGame: Moonshots. Liedtke explained that "players organize deliberate battles and exchange sacrificial fleets to help one another obtain those valuable moons. They have turned destruction into a cooperative project. For a designer, the lesson is to examine what players can achieve together, as well as what an individual action rewards."

As the team figured out how to develop "the more imaginative side of science fiction" in OGame's universe, they also decided to explicitly use deuterium for fusion research and as fuel. Star Trek fans will recognize this as the starship fuel of that universe, but it is a real substance: one of two stable isotopes of hydrogen. "Those scientific references give the universe familiar foundations," remarks Liedtke.

In OGame's shared galaxy, Orion is introducing "anomalies" as a central new feature, which Liedtke described as "mission sites you uncover with a new scanner" before it's required to send in ships. "Combat missions ask you to hold position against waves of automated fleets; peaceful missions put your cargo ships to work collecting rewards." The twist is these missions are open to co-op... but also to rival commanders that can attack the objectives marked as PvP. While you can theoretically ignore them, better rewards await for daring commanders.

With PvE bringing all sorts of new design opportunities to the table, Liedtke pointed out the Orion update "gives us a foundation to learn which kinds of missions players find rewarding" as GameForge looks to the strategy MMO's future. "Personally, I would like to explore encounters that make commanders reconsider what to send and how to work together. Discovery becomes more interesting when it changes your plan."

Sounds exciting, though Liedtke quickly added that this isn't an official announcement of future features.

OGame's 25th anniversary is in 2027, and while the team is tight-lipped on what the team has planned, Liedtke noted that "Reaching a quarter of a century in 2027 will be an extraordinary moment for OGame. We owe that longevity to the team's continued work and, above all, to the players who keep building empires, forming alliances, and giving this universe its stories."

OGame is available on PC (via browser and GameForge's own platform) and on mobile devices via the App Store and Google Play. The Orion update arrives on November 6, 2026.

#649. Perspective Films Reveals Inaugural Documentary Film Slate (EXCLUSIVE)

Perspective Films, a new documentary co-production initiative led by independent producer Jess Devaney, has unveiled its inaugural slate of films, Variety can report exclusively. The subjects of Perspective’s first five documentaries include the clash between federal immigration enforcement and the citizens of Minneapolis, the war in Gaza and the invention of C-SPAN.

“Every story on this slate is about who gets to shape history — a concert that sparked a movement, a network that threw open the halls of power to the public and residents documenting state violence as it unfolds,” Devaney said. “These films bring together Oscar-winning directors, veteran producers, and a journalist reporting from inside a war zone. They are collaborators of extraordinary talent and courage, and we’re proud to partner on their visionary films.”

Devaney, Perspective’s narrative strategist and the founder of Multitude Films, joined the label in May. Her previous works include “Life After,” “Pray Away” and “Power” for Netflix, the Emmy-winning “Lowndes County and the Road to Black Power” and HBO’s “How We Get Free.”

Perspective Films was built from the Perspective Fund’s Documentary Film Support program, which, under the leadership of program officer Andrew Catauro, offers grant funding for nonfiction projects. Selected titles receive up to $375,000 toward development, filming, post-production or distribution. Perspective Films also offers guidance at every step of the filmmaking process from conception to release.

See Perspective Film’s initial slate below.

“THEY’RE HERE,” which premiered at the Venice and New York Film Festivals this year, is a documentary that unfolds like a horror film that follows Edén Villa (a pseudonym) and anonymous Minneapolis residents as they evade and resist the paramilitary occupation of their city. Told in the tradition of dystopian cinema, “THEY’RE HERE” is set in a winter landscape where masked agents abduct children, residents travel in trunks, shackled prisoners are loaded onto airplanes within eyesight of vacationers and bicyclists track the movements of an invading force. Directed by Academy Award-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras and Minneapolis-based filmmaker Rachel Lauren Mueller. Produced by Rachel Lauren Mueller, Laura Poitras, Yoni Golijov. Screening at film festivals.

“THE PEOPLE’S NETWORK,” traces C-SPAN’s evolution of almost five decades from a bold experiment into an essential civic institution. After revolutionizing access to government in the age of cable, C-SPAN now faces a new era and a renewed question: how to best serve the public at a time when America needs it the most? Directed by Alyse Shorland; produced by Darcy McKinnon and Sara Archambault. In Production.

“UNTITLED GAZA DOCUMENTARY,” details embargoed until launch. Directed by anonymous. Produced, written and edited by Rabab Haj Yahya; produced by Ayah Selene and Munir Atalla. In post-production.

“FARM AID,” tells the story of Willie Nelson, Neil Young and John Mellencamp organizing what they thought would be a one-time benefit concert for small family farmers in 1985. Forty years later, the crisis has reached another breaking point and the movement that refused to let rural America disappear is still fighting. Directed by Kathlyn Horan; produced by Academy Award nominees Julie Goldman and Christopher Clements and Emmy winner J. Daniel Torres. In production.

“UNTITLED POLICING DOCUMENTARY” explores media and cultural portrayals of policing. Directed by Academy Award-nominated director Geeta Gandbhir; produced by Academy Award-nominated producer Alisa Payne. In development.

#648. A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history

In the hills of north-west Morocco, overlooking the river that gives the site its name, research at Oued Beht is bringing to light a previously unknown chapter of the region’s past. The discovery of a substantial built structure suggests that, during the second millennium BC, communities in north-west Africa were actively shaping their environment. They were also engaging in broader networks of interaction across the Mediterranean world.

Previous research by the Oued Beht Archaeological Project had already brought to light what is likely the earliest and largest agricultural complex ever discovered in Africa outside the Nile Valley. It dates to around 5,400 to 4,900 years ago. New excavations carried out in 2023 – in which we took part – have now deepened our understanding of the site.

Our new study shows how we uncovered the earliest known large-scale construction of a probably defensive nature in north Africa beyond the Nile Valley. It’s about 4,000 to 3,500 years old.

It’s not known exactly what threats these wall-like structures were designed to counter. They likely relate to increasing competition over land, resources, and possibly control of movement through the landscape, rather than to “invaders”. Constructions like these suggest communities felt the need to protect themselves or assert power over strategic locations.

This discovery pushes back the evidence for organized defensive architecture in the Maghreb and suggests that societies in this region at this time were more complex and structured than previously believed.

Our study also reveals how the ridge of Oued Beht would become a focal point again in the medieval period, during the 11th to 13th centuries AD. The same defensive structure was rebuilt, a hamlet or farm was established on a nearby hilltop, and people were buried in a cemetery between the two areas.

Together these findings provide rare archaeological insights into rural communities during both prehistoric and medieval times. They help us understand how societies developed and maintained themselves in a region too often left out of the history books.

For a long time, the later prehistory of north Africa’s Maghreb region (the Mediterranean countries of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia) has been poorly understood. Compared with neighboring areas such as Iberia in south-western Europe or Athens in the eastern Mediterranean, archaeological evidence was often fragmentary. In the last few years this has changed completely.

Excavations at Oued Beht have revealed a large concentration of human activity spread across at least ten hectares. The earliest major phase dates to the mid-fourth and early third millennia BC, or the Final Neolithic period.

Environmental evidence from plant and animal remains in the prehistoric era indicates a farming community cultivating crops such as barley and wheat. They also exploited wild plants and kept livestock.

The site was also an important center of craft production. Thousands of polished stone axes and other tools have been discovered, along with finely made pottery, sometimes decorated with painted patterns.

It’s still uncertain whether prehistoric Oued Beht functioned as a permanent village, a seasonal center, or something less familiar. But it was clearly a major focus in the landscape of north-west Morocco.

The presence of potentially ancient earthworks and walls had been noted since the 1930s. The French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann first documented a configuration of three walls, with the fourth side protected by the natural scarp of the ridge, describing a defensive éperon barré (barred spur). Their precise nature and date remained uncertain until now.

New excavations have clarified the existence of a multi-phase ditch, rampart and wall built across a narrow section of the Oued Beht ridge between the river and a ravine. This cut off and protected the ridge’s southern tip.

Radiocarbon dating of deposits associated with these structures gave us the timelines in our study.

They place its original construction at a time equivalent to the Bronze Age of the remaining western Mediterranean. This makes it the earliest confirmed defensive construction in north Africa outside Egypt.

This structure raises important questions about the society that built it. Building an embankment and ditch system required planning, coordination and the mobilization of labor. This suggests a community capable of organizing complex construction initiatives.

During the earlier Neolithic phase, activity at Oued Beht focused on the larger and more open northern area of the site. By the period of our new study, focus had shifted to the narrower, more defensible southern ridge. This may reflect a shift in settlement strategies.

The second millennium BC was a dynamic period across the Mediterranean. In southern Iberia, Argaric societies (about 2200-1550 BC) in today’s Europe were developing complex, often hilltop settlements. They were characterized by planned architecture, advanced metallurgy (especially bronze production), and marked social hierarchies visible in burial practices. These communities often constructed fortified sites, and strategically located settlements controlling surrounding territories.

Increasing evidence suggests that communities in north-west Africa were connected to wider Mediterranean networks. This includes today’s Spain and Portugal. The discoveries at Oued Beht indicate that the Maghreb was not isolated. It participated in broader processes shaping the western Mediterranean.

The defensive system at the site may reflect wider transformations in social organization and regional interaction. There may have been growing competition over resources, control of movement, and more formalized leadership structures.

The discoveries at Oued Beht highlight how much remains to be learned about the deep history of north Africa. The defensive wall shows that communities here were able to coordinate large construction projects and points to social transformations that are only very tentatively beginning to be recognized.

The medieval remains demonstrate that the ridge was used again many centuries after the prehistoric settlement had been abandoned. Oued Beht was not simply a single-period settlement but a landscape repeatedly selected by different communities across millennia.

As research continues, this location may become key to understanding how societies in the Maghreb evolved from early farming communities to the medieval rural world.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Giulio Lucarini, Cyprian Broodbank, and Toby C. Wilkinson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
